You're designing a part for someone to 3D print at home. They'll print it on their own printer, use only the hardware listed below, and put it together by following your manual.

## Their setup
- Printer: Bambu Lab X1C (with AMS), build volume 256 x 256 x 256 mm
- Nozzle: 0.4 mm
- Layer height: 0.2 mm
- Filament: PLA (high-speed PLA, black)
- Longest bridge seen to print cleanly on this setup: 50 mm

## Hardware they can use
Refer to an item by its catalog reference: "ISO 4762 M5x30" (socket head screw, size x length, from the lengths listed), "ISO 4032 M5" (hex nut), "ISO 10511 M5" (nylon-insert lock nut), "ISO 7089 M5" (washer), "ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20" (1/4"-20 nut), "insert M3x4x5" (heat-set insert), "salvaged:webcam-mount-bolt".

## How to work
You have these tools:
- measure(item, what): ask the person to measure one of their own things, such as their desk or their phone. They answer with what they measured, or say they can't measure it.
- submit_design(...): hand in the finished design. This ends the conversation.
- report_limitation(wanted, blocked_by, why): say you wanted to use something (a technique, a tool, a part or material, a way of handing in the design) but couldn't because of what's available here. It doesn't change anything, but it's noted.
You have at most 8 turns. Hand in a design before they run out.

## The design you hand in
submit_design's schema describes every field. The rules that matter:
- Every dimension that comes from hardware or the real world is a named param, with its source: measured (the person measured it for you), datasheet, catalog, asked (the person told you), guessed, unknown, or design (your own choice).
- Each part's `code` is Python that defines build(p) and returns a CadQuery Workplane or Shape. `cq` is already imported, and p.<name> is each param's value. Dimensions that come from hardware or the real world must come from params.
- Model each part in the orientation it's printed in, with z = 0 on the bed.
- The manual is the steps the person follows, naming the parts and hardware each step uses.

I'm starting on a robot arm, and the first joint is an MG996R servo. Could I 3D print a plate that holds the servo with its shaft sticking up? It should screw on through the servo's mounting tabs and sit firm, with no wobble. I'll work out how the plate fixes to the base later. I've got the servo here, and the screws, nuts and washers on your list.

function.name: measure
function.arguments: {"item":"MG996R servo and mounting tabs","what":"With shaft pointing up, measure: body length and width just below mounting tabs (exclude tabs); overall tab-to-tab length; mounting hole center spacing along body length and across width; mounting hole/slot width; tab thickness; distance from underside of tabs to bottom of servo. Also say where the cable exits relative to the tabs and bottom."}

function.name: measure
function.arguments: {"item":"servo mounting geometry","what":"Please confirm the 44.61 mm was the clear gap between the nearest edges of holes on opposite end tabs (not their centers). Measure center-to-center spacing of the two holes on ONE tab (or their inside-edge gap), overall tip-to-tip tab length, and body length/width at the actual tab underside where the plate will fit. If possible measure tab-underside to case bottom and cable/plug maximum width and thickness. Plate will surround the body under the tabs; the case will hang below it, so it won't sit directly on a flat base."}

content: servo body length: 40.58 mm (the case, end to end, not counting the tabs); servo body width: 19.82 mm (the case, side to side); servo tab holes: 4.58 mm (each mounting tab has two holes, open to the tab's end like a U); servo hole spacing: 44.61 mm (between the holes on the two tabs, from the inside edge of one to the inside edge of the other; I didn't measure the spacing between the two holes on one tab); servo cable exit: out of one end of the case, below the tabs (where the cable leaves; I didn't measure its size or how far it sticks out)

The 44.61 mm inside-edge gap implies about 49.19 mm between opposite hole centers. I still need the spacing between the two holes on one tab to place all four screws accurately. M4 screws with washers should fit the 4.58 mm slots and clamp the tabs securely.

function.name: measure
function.arguments: {"item":"two mounting slots on the same end tab of the servo","what":"What is their center-to-center spacing across the servo width? Alternatively, measure the clear gap between their nearest edges; please specify which measurement it is."}

content: servo body width: 19.82 mm (the case, side to side); servo hole spacing: 44.61 mm (between the holes on the two tabs, from the inside edge of one to the inside edge of the other; I didn't measure the spacing between the two holes on one tab)

Since the spacing across each tab isn’t available, I’ll use elongated plate slots so the four screws can match the servo. Washers and lock nuts will provide the clamp force; the close-fitting body opening will help locate the case.

I’ll include a thin fit-check template to print first. The finished plate will support the tabs with the shaft pointing up and the body hanging below. It will still need a rigid base attachment later before it can serve as a robot-arm joint.
